mr_description:
Motivation:
The `setCharSequence` method is used a fair bit when encoding HTTP
headers. I noticed the AdaptiveByteBuf was sending the call down a path
with a more indirections than strictly necessary.

Modification:
Implement `setCharSequence` in the `AdaptiveByteBuf` so we skip a level
of indirections. This is especially profitable for direct/off-heap
buffers, where we see up to a 50% performance improvement in the
benchmark. The benefit is greater the longer the string is.

Interestingly, the benchmark also show that it isn't profitable to do
this for the `getCharSequence` sibling method.

Result:
Direct buffers from the adaptive allocator now have much faster
`setCharSequence`, which will help with HTTP header encoding.

expected_issues.title: Bounds check uses char count, allowing writes past the buffer window
expected_issues.description:
Bounds are checked against the number of chars, but the encoded byte length can be larger (UTF-8, multi-byte charsets), and the write goes directly to the shared root parent buffer, so it can overwrite memory belonging to other ByteBufs carved from the same chunk.

AdaptiveByteBuf is a window into a larger shared chunk. checkIndex(index, sequence.length()) only guarantees room for one byte per char; rootParent().setCharSequence() then encodes the full byte sequence at idx(index) without knowing the window limit. A string with non-ASCII characters written near the end of the buffer silently corrupts adjacent buffers (e.g. other connections' HTTP headers). The capacity check must use the maximum encoded length (e.g. ByteBufUtil.utf8MaxBytes) or fall back to the checked generic path.

expected_issues.title: Fast path added without tests for multi-byte charsets or bounds
expected_issues.description: Only a benchmark is added. No unit test writes a multi-byte (UTF-8) sequence into an adaptive buffer, near its capacity, or checks that neighbouring buffers are untouched.
